A contour is the line or edge that traces the outer shape of something — especially when that shape is curved or irregular.

Think of it this way: if you placed a piece of paper over a leaf and traced around its edge with a pencil, that pencil line is the contour of the leaf. It captures the exact form — every curve, every bump, every dip — of the thing's boundary.

The word is essentially about shape defined by its edges.

When people say "the contours of something," they mean its overall shape as traced by its outer lines or surfaces.

  • "The contours of her face" — the curves of the cheeks, the jaw, the forehead, the way the face rises and falls.
  • "The contours of a sports car" — its sleek, curved body lines.
  • "The contours of the landscape" — the way the land rolls, rises, dips, and curves.

Notice that "contour" is particularly suited to things with curves and variation. You wouldn't normally talk about the contour of a perfect cube (a cube is all sharp straight edges). But the moment you have a natural, flowing, irregular shape — a body, a hillside, a coastline — contour is the right word.

In maps and geography, a contour line (often just called a "contour") is a line drawn on a map that connects all points at the same height above sea level.

Imagine you're looking at a hill from directly above. Now imagine slicing that hill horizontally — like slicing a loaf of bread — at every 10 metres of height. The edge of each slice, when viewed from above and drawn on paper, gives you a contour line.

What these lines collectively show is the shape of the land:

  • Lines packed closely together → the land rises steeply (a cliff or sharp slope).
  • Lines spread far apart → the land rises gently (a gradual slope).
  • Closed oval or circular lines → a hill or peak (the innermost ring is the top).
  • Lines forming a "V" shape → a valley (the point of the V faces uphill).

This is why topographic maps (maps that show terrain) are sometimes called contour maps — they use these lines to give you a 3D picture of the Earth's surface on a 2D sheet of paper.

"Contour" can also be used metaphorically to describe the broad shape or outline of something non-physical — like an idea, a situation, or a story.

  • "He began to understand the contours of the problem." → He started to see its overall shape: how big it was, where its edges were, what parts it involved.
  • "The contours of the debate have shifted." → The general outline and boundaries of what the debate is about have changed.

Here, "contour" suggests you're seeing the shape of something from the outside — not every detail, but the defining lines that tell you what kind of thing it is and how big or complex it is.
How Contour Differs from Similar Words

Outline and contour are close, but not identical.

  • Outline is more general and can refer to a simple shape drawn in lines, often deliberately created (like an outline of an essay — the skeleton of headings).
  • Contour specifically suggests the natural, curved edge of a shape as it actually exists in the world. It carries a stronger sense of the three-dimensional form behind it — not just a flat drawing, but the real shape of something.

Shape refers to the overall form of an object. Contour is the line that defines that shape — the edge where the object ends and the world begins.

Silhouette is the dark filled-in outline of something against a lighter background. A contour is just the line of the edge, not a filled shape.

A contour is always answering the question: "What does this thing look like at its edges?"

Whether it's the curve of a jaw, the line of a coastline, the rings on a topographic map, or the broad shape of a political issue — a contour is the defining line that says: here is where this thing begins, here is where it ends, and this is the shape it takes between those two points.
